title: Journal Examples for Students: 8 Samples + Models
description: Journal examples for students and college students: reflective journal samples, the Gibbs cycle and What? So what? Now what? explained, plus tips for marks.
intro: A student journal is a short piece of writing where you describe something you learned or did, then reflect on what it meant and what you will do next. Teachers usually want three things: what happened, what you think about it, and what you learned. Below are journal examples for students at school and college, plus the two reflection models most classes use.

writer.title: My reflection
writer.hint: What happened? So what does it mean? Now what will I do?

sections.h2: What teachers look for in a student journal

blocks.p: A class journal is not just a summary. Teachers want to see your thinking, not just repeat what was said in class. The best entries show that you understood something, questioned something, or changed your mind. A strong student journal entry:

ul: **Describes briefly.** One or two sentences on what happened. Do not retell the whole lesson.
**Reflects honestly.** How you felt, what surprised you, what confused you.
**Connects.** Links the experience to class ideas, readings or your own life.
**Looks forward.** Says what you will do differently or want to learn next.
**Uses "I".** Reflective journals are personal. First person is expected.

blocks.tip: Always check your teacher's instructions first. Some want a set length, a set model, or references to readings.

sections.h2: Model 1: What? So what? Now what?

blocks.p: This is the simplest reflection model and a favorite in schools. It has three questions:

ol: **What?** What happened? Describe the event or lesson in plain words.
**So what?** Why does it matter? What did you feel, notice or learn?
**Now what?** What will you do next because of it?

example.label: Student journal
example.title: Lab: testing enzymes
example.text:
What? We tested how heat changes enzyme activity in a lab.
So what? Our results at 60 degrees were way off.
I realized we did not wait the full five minutes.
Timing matters as much as the method.
Now what? Next lab, I will use a timer and record every step.

blocks.p: This model works for almost any subject: a science lab, a book chapter, a field trip, or a group project.

sections.h2: Model 2: Gibbs reflective cycle, in plain words

blocks.p: The Gibbs reflective cycle was created by Graham Gibbs in 1988. It is common in college courses like nursing, teaching and social work. It has six stages you go through in order:

steps.name: Feelings
steps.text: What were you thinking and feeling at the time?

steps.name: Evaluation
steps.text: What was good and what was bad about the experience?

steps.name: Analysis
steps.text: Why did things go the way they did? Link to what you have learned in class.

steps.name: Conclusion
steps.text: What else could you have done? What did you learn?

steps.name: Action plan
steps.text: If it happened again, what would you do?

example.label: Reflective journal
example.title: Talking to a worried parent
example.text:
Description: A parent asked me why her son was moved groups.
Feelings: I panicked. I did not know the answer.
Evaluation: I stayed polite, but I guessed instead of checking.
Analysis: In class we learned to refer up when unsure.
Conclusion: Saying "let me find out" is honest and fine.
Action plan: Next time, I will ask my mentor before replying.

blocks.tip: For a graded Gibbs reflection, the analysis stage usually earns the most marks. Link what happened to a reading, theory or lecture.

example.label: Reading journal
example.text:
In chapter 6, Scout finally sees Boo Radley as a person.
I was surprised how sad this made me.
It reminds me how fast we judge people we never talk to.
Question: does Scout change how she treats others after this?

example.label: Learning log
example.text:
Today: solving equations with fractions.
I got it once Ms. Lee showed multiplying both sides by the bottom.
Still confused: what to do when there are two different bottoms.
I will try problems 4 to 8 tonight and ask Thursday.

example.label: Project reflection
example.text:
Our group made a timeline of the civil rights movement.
I did the research. I felt like I did more than my share.
But I never told anyone. That is on me.
Next time I will suggest we split tasks on day one.

example.label: College journal
example.text:
Lecture on memory: we forget most new info within days.
That explains why cramming never works for me.
It matches the idea of spaced practice from the reading.
Plan: review notes for 10 minutes the day after each lecture.

example.label: Personal journal
example.text:
Midterms next week and I feel behind in everything.
Wrote it all down. It is really just chem and history.
Chem: two chapters. History: one essay.
That is doable. Starting chem tomorrow at 10.

blocks.p: For more non-school styles, see our main [journal examples](/journal-examples/) page.
Not every student journal is a graded reflection. Here are other kinds teachers use, and that students keep on their own.

ul: **Daily highlights journal:** the best moment of the school day.
**Gratitude journal:** good things, people and small wins.
**Project journal:** notes, progress and lessons for one big assignment, hobby or sport.
**School journal:** questions, homework and what you learned each week. It doubles as a planner.
**Dream journal:** dreams written down right after waking.
**Creative journal:** writing mixed with drawing, collage or poems.
**Feelings journal:** a private place for worries, friendships and stress.

example.label: Daily highlights
example.title: Best moment today
example.text:
At lunch we argued about which superhero would win a race.
I said The Flash. Everyone else said Superman.
We laughed so hard Maya spilled her juice.
Best part: the new kid joined in and now he sits with us.

example.label: Sports journal
example.text:
Coach had us run passing drills for an hour.
My left foot passes are still weak.
I will practice against the garage wall for 10 minutes a day.
Game Saturday. Nervous but ready.

sections.h2: Weak vs strong: the same entry two ways

blocks.p: The easiest way to improve a student journal is to compare a weak entry with a strong one about the same event.

example.label: Weak entry
example.text:
We went to the science museum.
We saw the dinosaur bones and the space room.
It was fun. Then we got back on the bus.

example.label: Strong entry
example.text:
At the science museum, the space room surprised me most.
I did not know light from some stars left them long ago.
It made the sky feel older and bigger than I thought.
It links to our unit on light speed.
I want to find out how scientists measure that distance.

blocks.p: The weak entry only lists events. The strong entry picks one moment, explains why it mattered, links it to class, and ends with a question. That is what teachers mean by reflection.

sections.h2: Reflective journal sample for students: phrases that help

blocks.p: Stuck on how to word it? These sentence starters fit most student journals:

ul: At first I thought... but now I think...
This surprised me because...
I felt... when...
This connects to what we learned about...
One thing I would do differently is...
I still have questions about...
Next time I will...

blocks.p: For prompts you can use each week, see [reflective journal prompts](/reflective-journal-prompts/). Younger students may like [journal prompts for teens](/journal-prompts-for-teens/).

sections.h2: Tips for a better student journal

ul: **Write soon after.** Reflect the same day while details are fresh.
**Be honest about mistakes.** Teachers reward real reflection more than perfect stories.
**Keep description short.** Spend most of your words on "so what" and "now what."
**Use one example.** Go deep on one moment instead of listing everything.
**Reread before you submit.** Check you answered every part of the assignment.

blocks.p: You can draft entries in our [free online journal](/online-journal-free/), then print or save as a PDF. Pages stay in your browser on this device.

faq.q: How do you write a journal entry for school?
faq.a: Start with the date and topic. Briefly describe what happened or what you learned. Then explain what you think about it, how it made you feel, and how it connects to class. End with what you will do next. The What? So what? Now what? model is an easy way to cover all three parts.

faq.q: What is a reflective journal for students?
faq.a: It is a journal where students write about their learning experiences and think about what they mean. Instead of just summarizing a lesson, you explain what you understood, what confused you, how you felt, and how you will use it. Many courses grade these entries.

faq.q: How long should a student journal entry be?
faq.a: It depends on the assignment. School journals are often 100 to 250 words. College reflective journals are often 300 to 800 words. If your teacher does not say, aim for enough to describe briefly and reflect in depth, and check the rubric.

faq.q: What is the Gibbs reflective cycle?
faq.a: It is a six-stage model for reflecting on an experience, created by Graham Gibbs in 1988. The stages are description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusion and action plan. It is widely used in nursing, teaching and other college courses to structure reflective writing.

faq.q: Can I use "I" in a reflective journal?
faq.a: Yes. Reflective journals are about your own thoughts and experiences, so writing in the first person is expected. Keep it clear and thoughtful, and support your points with examples or links to class material when asked.

faq.q: What are some journal ideas for college students?
faq.a: College students often keep reflective journals for placements, learning logs for hard courses, reading responses, and personal journals for stress and goals. Weekly prompts like "What idea changed how I think this week?" or "What am I struggling with and who could help?" work well. Keep entries honest and link them to what you are learning.
